progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Dm | Bb C | Dm Dm |
intro: A defence speech delivered to a judge. The heading calls it a prayer, tefillah, which only a handful of psalms in the book do, and everything after the first verse is either evidence, a request for cover, or a portrait of the prosecution. The grammar to watch is the object suffix on verbs: test me, refine me, answer me, guard me, hide me, surround me. The speaker is the object of almost every action in the psalm, God's and the enemies' alike. Track the body parts too, heart, lips, mouth, steps, feet, eye, ear, belly, and note that the last word of all is a face.

stichs.en: A prayer of David.
Hear a just cause, LORD,
listen to my cry,
give ear to my prayer, from lips with no deceit in them.

verses.summary: Three imperatives for listening stacked in one verse, each one louder than the last, and then the condition attached to the request: the mouth making it is clean.

stichs.en: Let my verdict come out from before You;
let Your eyes see what is straight.

verses.summary: The courtroom is named. The speaker does not ask to win, he asks for the case to be moved to a bench that sees straight.

stichs.en: You have tested my heart,
You have inspected it by night,
You have refined me and You find nothing:
I have resolved that my mouth will not overstep.

verses.summary: The evidence is that the audit has already happened. Three verbs of examination in the perfect tense, all of them completed, all of them God's.

stichs.en: As for what people do, by the word of Your lips
I have kept myself off the tracks of the violent.

verses.summary: The first claim about conduct rather than interior state, and the standard invoked is external: not conscience, but something spoken.

stichs.en: Hold my steps firm in Your ruts;
my feet have not slipped.

verses.summary: The image is a cart wheel staying in the groove of a road already worn by traffic. Innocence here is a matter of not drifting sideways.

stichs.en: As for me, I have called on You, because You answer me, God;
tilt Your ear toward me,
hear what I say.

verses.summary: The plea restarts here, and the reason given is past performance: he calls because answering is what this God does.

stichs.en: Make Your acts of kindness extraordinary,
You who save with Your right hand those who take shelter from attackers.

verses.summary: The request is not for kindness but for kindness beyond the usual measure. The verb is the one used for wonders, not for routine mercy.

stichs.en: Guard me like the little pupil of an eye,
hide me in the shadow of Your wings,

verses.summary: Two images of the smallest thing protected by the largest: an eye that closes reflexively, and a bird that spreads over what is under it.

stichs.en: from the wicked who have wrecked me,
my enemies, who ring me round with appetite.

verses.summary: The threat is finally named, and it is described as a closing circle rather than a single blow. The psalm will keep that circle shrinking for three more verses.

stichs.en: They have shut up their own fat;
with their mouth they speak arrogance.

verses.summary: Fat here stands for the insulated heart, sealed off so nothing gets in. Closed inside, open outside: the two halves of the verse are one diagnosis.

stichs.en: Our every step: now they have surrounded us;
they fix their eyes on bringing us down to the ground.

verses.summary: The pronoun goes plural for one verse only, us rather than me, and the steps of verse 5 come back with hunters standing on them.

stichs.en: He is like a lion aching to tear,
like a young lion sitting in the hiding places.

verses.summary: The circle collapses into one animal. Two ages of the same predator, one in the open wanting the kill, one waiting where it cannot be seen.

stichs.en: Rise, LORD,
meet him head on, force him to his knees;
let Your sword rescue me from the wicked.

verses.summary: The only verse where God is asked to move rather than watch. The verb for making him kneel is what a hunter does to an animal that is still standing.

stichs.en: From men, by Your hand, LORD,
from men of this passing world, whose share is in this life.
You fill their belly from what You have stored,
they have their fill of sons,
and leave what is left over to their small children.

glosses: and with what You have stored
verses.summary: The hardest verse in the psalm and one of the hardest in the book. It reads either as a complaint that the wrong people prosper or as a request that they be paid off in exactly this currency and no other.

stichs.en: As for me, in righteousness I will see Your face;
when I wake I will have my fill of Your form.

verses.summary: The last verse answers the previous one word for word: they are filled with sons and surplus, he is filled with a face. Both parties get what they were hungry for.

pardes.body: Read it as a case file. Verses 1 to 5 are the plea and the evidence, 6 to 9 the request for protective custody, 10 to 12 the description of the accused, 13 and 14 the sentence asked for, and 15 the closing line. The turn is at verse 9, where the danger stops being hypothetical and becomes a circle of people who are already moving. Notice that nothing in the psalm asks for the enemies to be removed from the picture; verse 13 asks that they be stopped, and verse 15 simply looks past them.

The psalm is held together by one root, the verb of being filled. {{14.10}} says the enemies have their fill of sons, and {{15.4}} says the speaker will have his fill of a face; the two forms are the same verb, and the whole argument of the psalm sits in the gap between the objects. The metallurgical verb of {{3.4}} belongs to an assayer purifying metal, so the claim is not that the speaker was found good but that he was put through fire and nothing burned off. Two disputed spots: {{9.5}} is literally with a soul or with an appetite, and translators split between calling these deadly enemies and calling them greedy ones. {{14.4}} is a rare noun that elsewhere means a lifespan or the duration of a life, which is why the same verse is rendered both as men of the world and as men of this fleeting age.

{{8.1}} to {{8.3}} pile up two separate words for the pupil, the little man and the daughter of the eye, and the shorter form of the phrase appears in the Song of Moses in Deuteronomy where God is said to guard Israel that way in the wilderness. Reading the psalm through that verse turns a private plea into a national one, and the plural us that appears once, in verse 11, is usually taken as the seam where that reading shows through. The verb of {{15.5}}, waking, carries the psalm's afterlife: the same verb is used in Daniel of those who sleep in the dust of the earth and wake, which is why the verse has long been read as being about resurrection rather than about morning. The plain sense, a man who has spent the night under examination in verse 3 and opens his eyes at dawn, is not thereby cancelled; both readings run in the tradition side by side.

The last word, {{15.6}}, is the word the Torah uses for a form or likeness, and it appears in two places that pull against each other: the second commandment forbids making any such form, and Numbers says of Moses alone that he looks at the form of the LORD. Deuteronomy insists that at Sinai the people heard a voice and saw no form at all. The psalm ends by claiming for its speaker what those texts reserve or deny, and the mystical reading takes the claim seriously rather than softening it: what is seen is not an image but the condition of a person who has been refined until there is nothing left in him that distorts. The night of verse 3 and the waking of verse 15 then frame the whole psalm as one passage through darkness, and the satisfaction of the final line is the state of a vessel that no longer leaks.
